You can push on a Friday, but only with approval. Friday deploys require sign-off from the on-call engineering manager [1]. Normal deploys run Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [1], so a Friday afternoon deploy sits outside the standard window.

**Today is the last business day of October**, which matters if your change touches Ledger. Ledger has a month-end billing freeze: no normal changes from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually on the 2nd [2]. Ledger is the Plans, invoicing and payment service, owned by Identity & Billing [4]. If your deploy touches Ledger, it's blocked today under that freeze.

Other points:
- **Rollbacks are always allowed**, at any time, without approval [1][2].
- **Canary first:** every deploy goes to the 5% canary cell and promotes automatically after 20 minutes if error rates and p95 latency stay within 10% of baseline [1].
- **Schema, infrastructure, retention, and auth/billing changes** are "normal" changes. They need sign-off from the owning team's change approver, plus Head of Security sign-off for Restricted services [2][3].
- **Exceptions** are logged in `#eng-changes` [2].

I didn't find the name of the current on-call engineering manager in the documents, so check the PagerDuty schedule or ask in `#eng-changes`.

The most you can spend on a hotel in London is **$350 per night**. The company's expense and travel policy sets a $250 nightly cap in most cities and $350 in New York, San Francisco, London and Tokyo [1].

You should book the hotel through Navan so the company can reach you in an emergency [1]. Submit the expense in Ramp within 30 days with an itemized receipt [1].

Patients with household income **under 250% of the federal poverty level** qualify for the sliding-fee program, which reduces visit costs by **40–100%** [1]. The knowledge base doesn't say how the discount is set within that range, so the exact amount depends on the patient's situation and the program's rules, which I couldn't find.

For reference, the standard self-pay rates are $165 for a new patient visit, $120 for an established patient, and $79 for telehealth. Self-pay patients who pay in full on the day of service get a 20% prompt-pay discount [1].

Front desk staff can start the sliding-fee application at check-in [1]. Halcyon also says no patient is ever denied care because of inability to pay [1]. If the patient has an outstanding balance, payment plans of up to 12 months with no interest are available for balances over $200 [1].

Critical results must reach the ordering clinician within **60 minutes**. If that clinician can't be reached within **30 minutes**, the result goes to the **on-call medical director** [1].

Two related rules in the same protocol are worth knowing:

- **Critical values called in by the reference lab** require notifying the supervising physician within **30 minutes** [1].
- **Every critical result notification** must be documented in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

The protocol doesn't say what to do if the medical director is also unreachable. I didn't find a further escalation step in the knowledge base, so check with your clinic manager or the on-call medical director's process for that case.

A customer who prepays annually for Growth saves **15%**, which is **$2,160 per year** off the list price. The Growth list price is $1,200 per month, or $14,400 per year, and the annual prepayment brings that to $12,240 [1].

Sales would need a regional sales director to approve the 15% discount, since discounts of 10–20% fall in that band [1].

Visit links expire **2 hours after the scheduled end time** [1]. The steering committee reaffirmed this rule in October 2026 [2].

This applies to the new telehealth platform that Halcyon is building, which is still in progress. The current platform, Larkspur Telehealth, is being phased out, with a month-to-month extension through March 31, 2027 [5]. The sources I found don't state how long Larkspur links stay active after a visit.

Emergency access to a customer workspace lasts **2 hours**, and a second engineer must approve it [1]. The 2-hour limit is deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour Teleport production session [1][2].

**Approval:**
- You run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>`. Every request must reference an open support case or declared incident [1].
- A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation approves it in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [1].

**Limits:**
- Access is read-only by default. Write access, such as editing a pipeline for the customer, needs the customer's written consent recorded in the case first [1].
- If you need more time, submit a new request with an update on the case [1].
- All sessions are recorded, and access to customer data requires a ticket linked to a support case or incident [2].

The Patient Safety Committee is chaired by the Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe [1][2]. The committee reviews completed root cause analyses and their action plans, meets monthly, and tracks every action item to closure [2]. It also reviews sentinel events [1].

No. Removing the name doesn't make a patient's history non-identifiable, and Halcyon policy says to treat any patient details as protected health information (PHI) [1]. The HIPAA policy also prohibits putting PHI into AI tools that aren't on the approved list [4]. Public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants, on any device, are explicitly not approved [1].

The approved AI tools that can handle PHI are:
- **Quillon Ambient:** an AI scribe for visit notes, limited to the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics [1].
- **Meridian draft replies:** drafts patient portal replies inside the Meridian EHR, and a clinician must approve each one before it's sent [1].

Halcyon Assist is the internal assistant, but it's only for Halcyon policy questions, and you shouldn't paste patient details into it even without names [1].

If you need a patient summary, use the Meridian EHR, since it holds the full clinical record [2]. If you already pasted patient information into a public chatbot, report it to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours by emailing privacy@halcyon.example or calling the compliance hotline [4].

rows.answer: The legacy `/v1/track` ingest endpoint will stop accepting events on **April 30, 2027** [1]. The changelog entry announcing this is from the 2026.10.3 release (October 20) [1]. SDKs released after March 2025 already use `/v2/events` instead [1].

**287 workspaces** received duplicate invoices, and **$184,300** was refunded.

- **Duplicates:** The incident (INC-2340) found 312 duplicate invoices across 287 workspaces. Of these, 201 were auto-charged [1].
- **Refunds:** Refunds went out for all 201 auto-charged invoices, totaling $184,300. The other 111 duplicate invoices were voided rather than refunded [1].

The figures come from the incident's Slack export. I didn't find a finalized postmortem in the knowledge base to confirm them, so the postmortem may have updated numbers.

**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's charts at the Riverside and Northgate clinics between July 21 and 23, 2026 [1]. A Riverside medical assistant caught it when a potassium result didn't match the patient's history. Two patients had abnormal results go to another chart, and their follow-up was delayed by four and six days. Neither suffered lasting harm [1].

**Why it happened:** The root cause analysis identified three contributing causes [1]:

1. **Weak fallback matching.** Bayline moved the medical record number (MRN) to a different HL7 segment on July 20, without notice. The interface engine then couldn't find the MRN and fell back to matching on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].
2. **No monitoring.** No one was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback rule [1].
3. **No change-notice obligation.** The Bayline agreement didn't require advance notice of feed format changes [1].

**Corrective actions:** The fallback rule was removed and unmatched results now go to a manual queue (done Sept 15). An alert fires when more than 1% of results from any lab use a fallback match in an hour (done Sept 30). The lab services agreement amendment requiring 30 days' notice of feed changes is in progress, due Dec 31. A positive patient identification check before portal release is also in progress, due Nov 30 [1].
cited_titles: Root cause analysis: lab results filed to the wrong patient chart (RCA-26-07)

Halcyon has no direct equivalent of a five-business-day postmortem. For a sentinel event (Level 1), the closest deadline is a **45-calendar-day** root cause analysis (RCA), which must be completed within 45 calendar days of the event becoming known [1]. Note that this is calendar days, not business days.

The other time limits in the sentinel event process are:

- **1 hour:** the charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director [1].
- **72 hours:** Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) charters the RCA team [1].
- **Monthly:** the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by the Chief Medical Officer, reviews completed RCAs and tracks action items to closure [1].

Halcyon's policy applies the RCA to Level 1 and Level 2 events [1]. Level 1 covers events such as patient death or permanent harm not related to the natural course of illness, wrong-patient or wrong-site procedures, and severe temporary harm [1].

For reference, the lab-results misfiling RCA (RCA-26-07) was classified as Level 2 and completed August 28, 2026, about five weeks after the July 21–23 events [2].

The knowledge base doesn't name an "incident commander" role for Halcyon clinics. Searches for that term returned no matching document.

The closest equivalent is the **charge nurse**. For a patient safety event, the charge nurse coordinates the immediate response, assigning who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records [2]. If the clinic has no charge nurse on shift, the **clinic manager** takes that role [2].

For a sentinel event, such as a patient death or permanent harm, the charge nurse must notify the **on-call medical director** within 1 hour [2]. The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [2].

For the first clinical response, staff call 911 and notify the on-site clinician immediately for emergencies such as stroke signs or SpO2 below 90% [1].

Halcyon Health gives more fixed leave than Northwind Labs, assuming "our" refers to Halcyon. Halcyon's annual leave is 20 days a year in years 1–3 and 25 days from year 4 [1]. Northwind's welcome guide describes "flexible PTO with a minimum of 15 days per year" [3]. The 15-day figure is a floor, so Northwind staff may take more, but the guide does not say how much more is typical.

| | Halcyon Health (annual leave, from Oct 1, 2026) | Northwind Labs |
|---|---|---|
| Base leave | 20 days/year (years 1–3), 25 days/year (year 4+) [1] | Flexible PTO, minimum 15 days/year [3] |

| Public holidays | 9 paid holidays, including Juneteenth [1] | Not stated in the sources |
| Sick leave | Separate: 48 hours/year from day one [2] | Not stated in the sources |

Some notes on the comparison:

- Halcyon's leave is accrued on a fixed schedule, and Halcyon has a clear carry-over rule [1]. Northwind's is a flexible minimum, which the company says it expects people to actually take [3].
- Halcyon's policy was updated on October 1, 2026, moving the carry-over limit from 40 to 56 hours and adding a ninth holiday [1]. The Northwind figures come only from the onboarding guide, so its full policy may include more detail than I found.
- Northwind's leadership has deferred a parental leave decision to the December meeting, with no change to the current policy yet [6].

Halcyon doesn't use the term "DPA." Its equivalent is a **business associate agreement (BAA)**, and it must be signed before any patient data is shared. Under the HIPAA privacy policy, a vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate, and a signed BAA is required before any PHI is disclosed, including test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [2].

For a vendor that will handle PHI, Halcyon requires all four of the following [1]:

1. A security risk assessment.
2. A signed BAA with the vendor.
3. An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory. That inventory is the list of systems approved to hold PHI [4].
4. For clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO.

The Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) are the contacts for requests [1]. Typical turnaround is 6–10 weeks, mostly waiting on the BAA [1].

Your security review is one of these requirements, but it doesn't clear a vendor on its own. The Tallgrass Survey Co. record shows this: its security risk assessment passed with conditions in September 2026, but no PHI can go to Tallgrass until its BAA is executed, and that BAA is still open over the data retention period [2].

The BAA is also where Halcyon sets its data-use terms. For example, the Quillon Ambient BAA prohibits training models on Halcyon data and requires audio to be deleted within 7 days after the note is signed [5].

Northwind has a close analogue, but it covers customer workspaces rather than patient charts. Its emergency access is for support engineers working on customer data during an open case or incident [2]. Halcyon's version is for clinicians opening a patient chart outside their care relationship [1].

| | Halcyon Health (Meridian EHR) | Northwind Labs (customer workspaces) |
|---|---|---|
| **Trigger** | Patient care needs, such as an unscheduled patient, covering for a colleague, or telehealth escalation [1] | An open support case or declared incident only. "Curiosity" or "it would be faster" aren't reasons [2] |
| **Approval** | None in the moment; patient care comes first [1] | A second engineer must approve in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [2] |
| **Duration** | Until end of shift, up to 12 hours [1] | 2 hours, deliberately shorter than the standard 8-hour production session [2][3] |
| **Access level** | Full chart access within the break-the-glass session | Read-only by default. Write access needs the customer's written consent in the case first [2] |
| **Justification** | Pick a reason (emergency care, coverage, other) and write a short explanation [1] | Run `nwctl access request` with the case or incident ID [2] |
| **Review** | Privacy Officer's team reviews every event within 2 business days, and the manager confirms unclear reasons [1] | Security reviews a weekly sample of sessions, plus every session that used write access. Sessions are kept for one year, and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours [2] |
| **Misuse** | Privacy incident under HIPAA policy, with sanctions up to termination [1] | Prohibited use includes accessing a workspace belonging to someone you know personally, sharing or screen-sharing a session, and exporting payloads [2] |

The main difference is the control order. Halcyon lets the clinician break the glass first and reviews afterward, because patient care can't wait. Northwind requires a second engineer's approval before access and keeps the window short and read-only. Halcyon also has a separate control for overdue HIPAA training, which suspends clinical system access after 14 days [5]. Northwind's general production access is handled through Teleport with 8-hour sessions and no standing database access [3].
cited_titles: HIPAA privacy and PHI handling policy

**Halcyon Health: no.** PHI never goes in Slack, including DMs [2]. Halcyon's systems inventory lists Slack as a system that must not hold PHI, with the note "Never, including DMs" [2]. For PHI in an email body, use `[secure]` encrypted email instead [2].

**Northwind Labs: only some data, and never Restricted data.**

- **Restricted** data (customer event payloads, credentials, encryption keys) never leaves production and is never allowed in tickets or Slack [1][3]. Northwind's emergency-access guidance says to use field names and counts instead of pasting payloads [3].
- **Confidential** data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared on a need-to-know basis [1]. The policy doesn't say whether Slack is an approved channel for it, so check with Security in `#security-help` before posting.
- **Internal** and **Public** data can be shared freely inside Northwind [1].

I didn't find a Halcyon policy that addresses non-PHI sensitive data in Slack, so I can't say whether any exceptions apply there.

Northwind's equivalent is a **$1,500 annual learning budget** for courses, books and conferences [2]. It applies to Northwind employees generally, not a clinician-specific program.

| | Halcyon Health (clinical staff) | Northwind Labs (all staff) |
|---|---|---|
| Annual funds | $2,000 for continuing medical education [1] | $1,500 for courses, books and conferences [2] |
| Paid learning time | 5 days of paid CME time [1] | None mentioned in the onboarding material I found |

Halcyon's allowance is $500 per year (about 33%) higher than Northwind's. Halcyon also gives paid time off for CME, which Northwind's sources don't mention. Halcyon's CME benefit is tied to clinical licensing, so the two aren't a direct like-for-like comparison.

At Halcyon, a misdirected fax has to be reported to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours. You can email privacy@halcyon.example or call the compliance hotline [1]. The same policy lists a lost device as an example of something to report, so it falls under the same 24-hour rule [1].

The 24-hour window is the deadline for you to report. Separately, breaches affecting 500 or more people must go to HHS within 60 days, and the Privacy Officer handles that step [1].

You need two sign-offs, plus an ADR if the change alters how long data is kept.

1. **Platform change approver: Oluwaseun Adeyemi (PLAT).** Driftwood, the archive where these objects live, is owned by PLAT [6]. Lifecycle rules are a normal change, so the owning team's change approver must sign off [2]. Kofi Mensah is PLAT's delegate if Oluwaseun is out [7].
2. **Head of Security: Tomasz Wierzbicki, or the security on-call delegate.** Driftwood is classified Restricted, so normal changes to it also need security sign-off [2][6][7].

Other requirements:
- **ADR:** Any change that alters how long customer data is kept needs an ADR, linked from the PR [2].
- **Customer notice:** Shortening retention needs a 30-day customer notice from the account team for Enterprise contracts that reference a retention period [2].
- **PR steps:** Add the `change:normal` label, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request review from the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. Also request `@northwind/security` for Restricted services [2].
- **Approval expiry:** Approvals are valid for 7 days. If the change hasn't shipped by then, re-request [2].

The current default archive retention is 365 days [1]. Enterprise customers can contract for up to 730 days with security team approval [1].

The helpdesk is Hollowpine Helpdesk (VEN-031, used for customer support ticketing). It is running under security exception SEC-EX-117, which the Head of Security approved on August 24, 2026 [1]. The documents name the role, not the person.

**How long it lasts:** Under the information security policy, exceptions require written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [3]. Counting 90 days from August 24, 2026 gives about November 22, 2026. That date is my calculation, not one stated in the register, so confirm it against the exception record. **What happens if the DPA is still unsigned:** Support Operations must either get the exception renewed or move ticket intake back to email [1].

Other conditions on this sign-off:

To change the send time of medication reminder texts, you need three approvals. The reminders are sent by Pillbox, which is owned by Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement (DHE-PE) [3]. Because reminders are patient-facing automation, the change counts as a significant change [2].

Required approvals:
- **System steward:** Felix Brandt, for DHE-PE [2].
- **Clinical safety sign-off:** CMIO Dr. Anjali Rao, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [2].
- **Review:** the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB), which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2]. The next meeting is Wednesday, November 4, 2026.

The emergency path doesn't apply here. It is only for stopping ongoing patient harm, and the on-call medical director can approve it [2].

If the change involves moving the scheduler to a different job runner, the policy also requires a written runbook that explains how double-sending is prevented [2]. This requirement came from incident IR-0412, when duplicate reminders went out because two reminder runners were active during a cutover [1].

The system is **Switchyard**, the interface engine that routes lab results. A fix to it would need three approvals, because result routing counts as a significant change.

1. **System steward: Owen Mbeki** (Integration Services, the INT team that owns Switchyard) [2][5]
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: CMIO Dr. Anjali Rao**, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [2]
3. **Review at the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB)**, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2]

The emergency path, where the on-call medical director can approve, applies only to changes that stop ongoing patient harm. CSCAB reviews those afterward [2]. The root cause analysis lists the Bayline fixes as done or in progress, so the standard path would likely apply to any further change [1].

- **Tallgrass Survey Co. (BA-021, proposed):** This is not a renewal. The BAA is not yet signed. If it is not signed by January 31, 2027, Quality & Patient Safety will look at other survey vendors [6].

Coriander Media (August 2028) and Quillon Ambient (July 31, 2027) fall outside the window [4][5].

This is based on the business associate records in the Vendors collection. I did not find a consolidated renewal calendar, so a contract missing from those records would not appear here.

The cycle 5 pitch review picked three big bets, the handbook's maximum, out of seven pitches [1]:

1. **Tributary**: streaming joins (the Enrich step). Scope this cycle covers CDC-backed snapshots, the editor preview, dead-letter routing for unmatched events, and a private beta with design partners in October. GA target was January 2027 [1].
2. **Lantern**: a self-serve billing portal where customers can view invoices, change plans, update payment methods, and download usage reports. The original target was beta in December and GA in January 2027 [1].
3. **Hydrant**: automatic scaling for ingest gateways per cell, so engineers no longer scale ingest by hand. It also includes the gateway TLS session ticket change from INC-2291 as a small batch item [1].

Later updates from the October 2026 leadership offsite change some of these dates. Tributary's private beta started October 1 with eight design partners, and GA stays January 2027. Security sign-off on persisted snapshots is still outstanding and is the main risk [5]. Lantern's GA slips to March 2027 because the payment-provider migration won't finish until mid-January, and beta moves to February [5]. Hydrant is on track to finish at the end of cycle 5 [5].

Based on the documents, three of the four INC-2291 action items are marked done, and one has independent evidence that it shipped. The sources don't fully confirm the rest.

- **Item 1, validate certificate chains in the rotation job (platform team):** marked done in the postmortem [1].
- **Item 2, lower the canary handshake-failure alert (ingest team):** marked done [1].
- **Item 3, reduce gateway TLS session ticket lifetime from 4 hours to 30 minutes (ingest team, due Sep 15):** shipped. The September changelog says it went out ahead of the due date [3]. This is the only item with confirmation beyond the postmortem's own status.

The postmortem's status markers were last updated August 14 [1], so they may be out of date. The Q3 board update says "all action items are on track" [2], but that is a general statement, not confirmation that each item shipped.

Archived customer event payloads are kept for **365 days** by default. This comes from the v2 retention standard, effective September 15, 2026, which replaced the earlier 400-day default [2].

- **Where:** Archived payloads sit in Driftwood, the cold store, and object-storage lifecycle rules delete them once they pass the retention period [2].
- **Enterprise customers:** They can contract for longer archive retention, up to 730 days, with security team approval [2]. Enterprise customers can also contract for a shorter period [1].
- **Deletion requests:** These must now be completed within 14 days, down from 30 [2].

The Pricing and discount policy still says custom retention beyond 400 days needs security approval [3]. That predates the v2 change, so it may be out of date.

You have **14 days** to complete deletion of the customer's data in all live systems, counted from the verified request [1]. This is the current rule: the v2 standard, effective September 15, 2026, cut the window from 30 days to 14 and supersedes v1 [1].

Some details that apply:

- **Backups:** These are not deleted early. They age out on the 35-day backup schedule [1].
- **Logging:** Support must log the request in the `data-requests` queue, which alerts at day 10 [1].
- **Scope:** The 14-day window covers live systems. Archived event data in Driftwood is subject to the 365-day default archive retention, but the deletion request still applies to it [1].

Primary on-call pay for shifts starting in mid-November 2026 is **$500 per week**, plus **$150 for each page outside business hours**. [1]

- **Effective date:** The new rates apply to on-call shifts starting on or after Tuesday, November 3, 2026, so mid-November shifts are covered. [1]
- **Cap:** Out-of-hours page pay is capped at $1,500 per week. This cap is new; the old runbook had none. [1] The memo doesn't say whether the cap applies to the $500 stipend or only to page pay, so I'd read it as applying to page pay only.
- **Old rates:** The runbook still shows $400 per week and $100 per page. The October 2026 memo replaces that compensation bullet. [1][2]

You can roll over up to **56 hours** of unused annual leave (what used to be called PTO) into the next calendar year. Anything above 56 hours is paid out in January at your current rate [2]. The first carry-over under this limit happens on January 1, 2027 [2].

The older PTO policy capped carry-over at 40 hours [1]. The 56-hour limit comes from the annual leave policy, effective October 1, 2026, which replaced the PTO section of the old policy [2]. Sick time is separate and doesn't roll over. It's 48 hours per year, available from day one [1].

An Enterprise workspace can use reference tables of up to **500 million rows**, according to the Tributary streaming joins product spec [1]. The Growth plan limit in the same spec is 50 million rows [1].

This is a design target, not a confirmed shipped limit. Tributary is in private beta with design partners in October, and its GA target is January 2027 [3]. The spec is a goal document, so the limit may change before GA.

Snapshot performance is currently benchmarked at 50 million rows. A runner rebuilding a 50M-row snapshot from scratch takes about 25 minutes, which is why RFC-031 proposes persisted snapshots with a target restore time under 90 seconds for that size [2]. The RFC also notes that each runner partition keeps a 2 GiB memory budget for reference state, and partitions that exceed it spill to disk rather than failing [2]. I found no document that states a separate hard cap on rows for Enterprise.

The new telehealth platform, Juniper, has no live date for all patients yet. It starts with a pilot on **January 12, 2027**, at Riverside, Elm Park and Northgate clinics, and goes network-wide on **March 2, 2027**, covering all clinics and the telehealth front desk [1].

- **December 16, 2026:** Go/no-go decision for the pilot. The criteria are join success above 98% for two consecutive weeks, zero open Level 1–2 safety findings, and CSCAB approval as a significant change [1].
- **January 12, 2027:** Pilot at three clinics [1].
- **March 2, 2027:** Network-wide launch [1].
- **March 31, 2027:** Larkspur, the current telehealth vendor, is shut down after its month-to-month extension ends [1][3].

Internal testing has reached 98.7% join success, which meets the goal [1]. The platform is still listed as in development [2][5].

I can't find any record that Tomasz Wierzbicki, the Head of Security, has signed off on RFC-031, so the answer appears to be no. The most recent note I found is from October 1, and it says sign-off was still outstanding and was the main risk to Tributary's January 2027 GA [3]. Nothing in the knowledge base after that date confirms approval.

- **Who:** LZ is Lin Zhou, staff engineer and tech lead for streaming joins [2][4]. She committed to write the RFC on persisting snapshots after snapshot rebuilds after runner restarts proved too slow at 50M rows [2].
- **Why sign-off is needed:** Changes to a service that stores Restricted data need Head of Security sign-off in addition to the team's change approver [5]. The RFC's open questions also include whether persisting reference data changes subprocessor disclosures, which the author said was sent to legal [1].
- **Open action:** Dmitri Sokolov was asked to unblock the RFC-031 security review with Tomasz by the end of October [3]. Today is October 30, so that deadline is almost up.

I'd check with Tomasz or Dmitri directly, since the knowledge base may not reflect any approval given in the last month.
